A ledger of stream positions keyed by SERVICE, with a CHECK naming three domains. Zero rows by construction: no reader and no writer in its whole life, established by census over its columns — `last_event_id` occurs exactly once in the tree, in this table's own declaration. It is the most dangerous of the four cursor tables for what its key says: keyed by subscriber it would invite one service to hold the position; keyed by service it reads as a CENTRAL ledger in which iam tracks how far each domain has read, so picking it up would reverse the decision for the whole platform and add an edge from a leaf back to the domains that the topology does not allow. That it was never widened is visible in the constraint itself: it names three domains (`vpc`, `compute`, `loadbalancer`) while the tree holds seven services — `storage`, `registry`, `geo` and iam itself never entered the list, and none of the 143 migrations preceding this one ever touched the constraint. NOT evidence, stated so the next reader does not derive it again as this entry's author did and was refuted at review: `loadbalancer` looks stale beside the `services/nlb` directory but is not — it is the platform's own domain name (proto package `kacho.cloud.loadbalancer.v1`, binary `kacho-loadbalancer`). On that axis the constraint AGREES with the platform; only the incompleteness of the list shows the lag. The position of a subscription belongs to the CLIENT, which is what lets a stream survive reconnecting to a different replica.

A replay ledger for proof-of-possession, created by the base schema and never written to since. Zero rows by construction: writers and readers in the non-test tree are zero, no migration in this chain INSERTs into it, and iam exposes no surface on any listener through which a row could be made. What this drop does NOT mean, stated first because the table's name reads as a protection: replay protection is ALIVE and untouched, it lives at the edge in `kacho_gateway.dpop_replay` under the edge's own migration 20260822140000. This table was never its store. It is more dangerous than an ordinary dead table because it carries the FULL shape of a replay ledger — proof id, seen-at, verb, address, key thumbprint — so a reader of iam's schema concludes iam holds single-use state, and both roads from that conclusion are wrong: treat the edge's store as a duplicate and remove it, or add a second writer here. The second is worse, because one mechanism in two schemas of two services is decided by two clocks and two windows, and single-use is a property of ONE decision: once the two stores disagree, a proof passes that either of them alone would have refused.

The version of the authorization model as LOADED INTO THE EXTERNAL RELATIONSHIP ENGINE, created by the base schema. The engine was retired by line R7-3 — the verdict is now computed by the relational form in the service's own database — so there is nowhere left to load a model and nothing left to write this row: writers and readers in the non-test tree are zero, and no migration in this chain INSERTs into it. What the drop does NOT mean, stated first because the name reads as model versioning: the DSL the relationship model is written in OUTLIVED the engine and is parsed by the service itself; the model text remains the source of truth for the shape. What goes is the record of a LOAD into a foreign store, not the versioning of the model. It is more dangerous than an ordinary dead table because it carries the full shape of a deployment journal — model id, DSL digest, applied-at, applied-by — so a reader of the schema concludes that model changes are recorded somewhere, and both roads from that conclusion are wrong: hunt for a writer that does not exist, or add a second one and thereby create a second place about one subject. Three objects go with the table and are counted with it: the sequence fga_model_version_id_seq (declared OWNED BY the column), the primary key and the unique key on the model id.
